newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish army says Islamists now enemy number one.
newsitem.headline: Turkish army says Islamists now enemy number one.

text.p: Turkey's armed forces have trained their heavy guns on Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, designating his Islamist supporters -- rather than any foreign power -- the biggest security threat facing the nation.

The secularist generals used a rare briefing with Turkish and foreign journalists, designed to project their side of a growing feud with Erbakan and his Islam-based Welfare Party, to announce a dramatic "inward" turn to their stratetic planning.
General Kenan Deniz said NATO-member Turkey's strategic threat assessment had been modified to concentrate on internal enemies, in place of old Cold War adversaries or regional rivals such as Greece.

"Actions directed at warding off the external threats were basically the first priority but after the collapse of the Soviet Union...there have been reassessments," he said. "The first priority is the domestic threat of separatism and fundamentalism.
"Destroying fundamentalism is of life or death importance," Deniz told the assembled journalists, as three functionaries from the foreign ministry nodded in agreement from a table below the rostrum.

Analysts say that by raising the rhetorical temperature the military brass clearly hope to entice defectors from Erbakan's coalition and "bleed" his 10-month-old government. Already two conservative ministers have resigned, with others wavering.
"It is the 'death of a thousand cuts'," said one Western diplomat. "Each public attack takes a little more of a toll until the victim collapses and dies."
"The name of the threat is: Fundamentalism," said a banner headline on Wednesday in the daily Milliyet, summing up the generals' presentation. "Shocking Briefing," said Hurriyet.

The army assured its listeners the danger of Kurdish separatism in the southeast had been largely contained, in a bloody 12-year fight that has claimed more than 22,000 lives. But the struggle with Islamist activism was less certain.
"This is not like the Cold War times where the enemy was definite and the general staff policy was in alliance with NATO," foreign affairs commentator Sami Kohen told Reuters.
"Now they (the soldiers) have to adjust themselves to the current situation which is the fundamentalist threat," he said.
Such manoeuvring is new to Turkey's generals, better known for bringing down three civilian governments since 1960 with more the direct method of sending tanks into the streets.

This time, they have launched a "creeping coup" -- most date it back to February 28 when the army first publically directed Erbakan implement an anti-Islamist crackdown -- better tailored to the last decade of the 20th Century.

"It is true that the soldiers do not want and will not carry out one of the classic coups known to us. This time we are faced with a different pattern. The coup has actually begun," said Bekir Coskun in the daily Hurriyet.

"The soldiers have found this method and are applying it after thinking about domestic and foreign balances, the economy being on a knife edge, Turkey being watched carefully by the whole world and about how much damage would be done to the country by anti-democratic images," Coskun said.
However, the calculations on the part of the military establishment also reflect the failure of Turkey's other political institutions, most notably the squabbling parties.
The secularist political elite proved unable to keep Erbakan from power despite his plurality of just 21 percent in the latest general election.
Now it appears increasingly unable to do anything to ease fears of greater Islamist penetration of public and political life -- except turn back to the army with nostalgic longing.
Clearly frustrated the generals stepped in with public demands that Erbakan crush the Islamists who make up his core voters, setting in motion the current crisis.
Veteran left-wing leader Bulent Ecevit was forced to admit on Wednesday that two other opposition figures had only loosely agreed to his formula for an "Islamist-free" government.

And personal rivalry -- not policy differences -- divide the leaders of two conservative parties. One, the True Path Party of Tansu Ciller, preferred coalition with Erbakan's Islamists than working with its main secularist rival, the Motherland Party.
